'''Marion Frederick Hawthorne''' (August 24, 1928 – July 8, 2021)<ref>{{Cite web|last=Katsnelson|first=Alla|date=July 12, 2021|title=Fred Hawthorne, inorganic chemist nicknamed Mr. Boron, dies|url=https://cen.acs.org/people/obituaries/Fred-Hawthorne-inorganic-chemist-nicknamed/99/web/2021/07|access-date=2021-07-14|website=cen.acs.org}}</ref> was an [[inorganic chemist]] who made contributions to the chemistry of [[Boranes|boron hydrides]], especially their [[Cluster chemistry|clusters]].

==Early life and education==
Hawthorne was born on August 24, 1928, in [[Fort Scott, Kansas|Fort Scott]], [[Kansas]]. He received his elementary and secondary education in Kansas and Missouri. Prior to high school graduation, he entered the [[Missouri University of Science and Technology|Missouri School of Mines and Metallurgy]], [[Rolla, Missouri]] through examination as a chemical engineering student. He then transferred to [[Pomona College]], where he received a B.A. degree in chemistry in 1949. While there he conducted research with [[Corwin Hansch]]. Hawthorne completed his Ph.D. in [[organic chemistry]] under [[Donald J. Cram]] at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in 1953. He conducted postdoctoral research at [[Iowa State University]] with [[George S. Hammond]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hawthorne|first=M Frederick|date=2013-04-01|title=Interview with M Frederick Hawthorne|journal=Future Medicinal Chemistry|volume=5|issue=6|pages=627–632|doi=10.4155/fmc.13.49|pmid=23617426 |issn=1756-8919|doi-access=free}}</ref> before joining the Redstone Arsenal Research Division of the [[Rohm and Haas|Rohm and Haas Company]] in [[Huntsville, Alabama|Huntsville]], [[Alabama]].

==Professional career==
At the Redstone Arsenal, he worked on the chemistry of boron hydrides making several notable discoveries.  In 1962, he moved to the [[University of California, Riverside]] as professor of chemistry. He moved to the [[University of California, Los Angeles|University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)]] in 1969. In 1998, he was appointed University Professor of Chemistry at UCLA.  He then returned to his home state of Missouri as head of the International Institute of [[Nanomedicine|Nano]] and Molecular Medicine at [[University of Missouri]].

Hawthorne was long associated with the journal [[Inorganic Chemistry (journal)|''Inorganic Chemistry'']], and was its longest serving editor-in-chief.

== Research ==
:[[File:Dodecaborate(12)-dianion-from-xtal-3D-bs-17.png|thumb|The dodecaborate anion ([B<sub>12</sub>H<sub>12</sub>]<sup>2−</sup>) was discovered by Pitochelli and Hawthorne.]]

Hawthorne's contributions focused on the chemistry of [[Boranes|boron hydride]] clusters.  He discovered [[dodecaborate]] anion (B<sub>12</sub>H<sub>12</sub><sup>2−</sup>)<ref>Anthony R. Pitochelli, Frederick M. Hawthorne "The Isolation of Icosahedral B<sub>12</sub>H<sub>12</sub><sup>2−</sup> Ion" J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1960, volume 82, pp 3228–3229.{{doi|10.1021/ja01497a069}}</ref> and metal complexes of the [[dicarbollide]] anion.<ref>M. F. Hawthorne, D. C. Young, P. A. Wegner, "Carbametallic Boron Hydride Derivatives. I. Apparent Analogs of Ferrocene and Ferricinium Ion"  J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1965, volume 87, pp. 1818–1819.  {{doi|10.1021/ja01086a053}}</ref>  His group subsequently discovered the perhydroxylation of B<sub>12</sub>H<sub>12</sub><sup>2−</sup>.<ref>M. W. Lee, Jr., A. V. Safronov,
S. Jalisatgi, M. F. Hawthorne "Cesium dodecahydroxy-closododecaborate, Cs<sub>2</sub>[B<sub>12</sub>(OH)<sub>12</sub>]" Inorg. Syntheses 2010, volume 35. {{doi|10.1002/9780470651568.ch2}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Hawthorne has been widely recognized, including with election to the US [[National Academy of Sciences]].

* 1992 – [[Honorary degree|Honorary doctorate]] from the Faculty of Mathematics and Sciences at [[Uppsala University]], [[Sweden]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.uu.se/en/about-uu/traditions/prizes/honorary-doctorates/mathematics-and-science/ |title=Honorary Doctors of the Faculty of Mathematics and Science |access-date=January 18, 2018 |publisher=Uppsala University }}</ref>
* 1994 – [[Chemical Pioneer Award]] from the [[American Institute of Chemists]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theaic.org/award_winners/chem_pioneer.html#cpa60s|title=Chemical Pioneer Award|publisher=American Institute of Chemists|access-date= 30 November 2015}}</ref>
* 2009 – [[Priestley Medal]] from the [[American Chemical Society]]<ref>{{cite news |url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/news/86/i25/8625notw1.html |title=Hawthorne is 2009 Priestley Medalist |newspaper=[[Chemical & Engineering News|C&EN]] |date=June 18, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404125431/http://pubs.acs.org/cen/news/86/i25/8625notw1.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 4, 2016 |first=Stephen K. |last=Ritter }}</ref>
* 2011 – [[National Medal of Science]]<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://munews.missouri.edu/news-releases/2012/1227-president-obama-honors-mu-researcher-with-national-medal-of-science/ |title=President Obama Honors MU Researcher with National Medal of Science |publisher=University of Missouri News Bureau |date=December 27, 2012 |access-date=January 18, 2018 |first=Timothy |last=Wall }}</ref>
